[16:00] ADITYA VERMA: Suresh, thanks for the quick turnaround. I've read the
ticket. Before we go into the substance, I want to understand the deadline
pressure. When do you file?

[16:00] SURESH IYER: The return is due on the twentieth of next month, but I
need the invoices reconciled by the fifth to give our accountant time. So
roughly eight days.

[16:01] ADITYA VERMA: Understood. That's a real constraint and I'll work to
it. Tell me what you found.

[16:01] SURESH IYER: We have 1,240 invoices for decorative lighting SKUs
issued at eighteen percent. They should be at twelve. The difference is
INR 2,17,600. Every affected SKU was listed after the first of February.

[16:02] RAHUL SHARMA: I confirmed that yesterday. SKUs listed before the
revision are correctly at twelve. Only the later ones are wrong. So the
calculation is fine, it's the mapping.

[16:03] SURESH IYER: That's what I concluded too. Which is why I'm not
angry about a system error. I'm concerned about what you're going to do
about the documents.

[16:03] ADITYA VERMA: Say more.

[16:03] SURESH IYER: If you just credit me the difference as an adjustment,
I still have 1,240 incorrect tax documents in my records. My auditor will
ask why the invoices don't match the returns. I need credit notes against
those specific invoices, and corrected invoices.

[16:04] ADITYA VERMA: So a net adjustment is not acceptable.

[16:04] SURESH IYER: Correct. It solves your accounting problem, not mine.

[16:05] ADITYA VERMA: That's a clear position and I think it's the right
one. Rahul, is there any reason we can't issue credit notes?

[16:05] RAHUL SHARMA: None that I know of. It's a question of who absorbs
the 2,17,600 and how it's recorded, which is your decision, not mine.

[16:06] ADITYA VERMA: Then let me deal with the part you're both waiting on.
Who absorbs it.

[16:06] SURESH IYER: I have a view, if you want it.

[16:06] ADITYA VERMA: Please.

[16:05] RAHUL SHARMA: None that I know of. It's a question of who absorbs
the 2,17,600 and how it's recorded, which is your decision, not mine.

[16:06] ADITYA VERMA: Then let me deal with the part you're both waiting on.
Who absorbs it.

[16:06] SURESH IYER: I have a view, if you want it.

[16:06] ADITYA VERMA: Please.

[16:07] SURESH IYER: The invoice is generated by your platform. The rate is
set by your mapping. I never touch it. If my team had made the error I would
absorb it without argument. But we didn't.

[16:07] ADITYA VERMA: I agree. We generate the document, so accuracy is
ours. That's consistent with our settlement policy and it's how I'd argue it
internally if I needed to.

[16:08] SURESH IYER: I appreciate you saying that plainly. I've had vendors
argue the opposite.

[16:08] ADITYA VERMA: I'll still need to get it approved, because it's
INR 2,17,600. But I'll put the recommendation in today and I'll tell you if
there's any resistance.

[16:09] SURESH IYER: Fair. And the timing?

[16:09] ADITYA VERMA: My target is credit notes issued by the fifth, so you
have them before your reconciliation deadline. That depends on operations
executing and the mapping being fixed first.

[16:10] RAHUL SHARMA: The mapping fix is straightforward. The operations tax
desk already corrected the classification for the affected SKUs yesterday.
The open question is the control.

[16:10] ADITYA VERMA: Go on.

[16:11] RAHUL SHARMA: Right now a new listing whose tax category resolves to
the default gets the default silently. That's how this happened. The fix is
to block publication and route it for classification.

[16:11] ADITYA VERMA: How much work does that create?

[16:11] RAHUL SHARMA: A small queue. Genuinely new product types need
classifying. Everything else resolves explicitly. In testing it was about
one to two listings a week across the platform.

[16:12] ADITYA VERMA: That's acceptable. Blocking is the right default. Add
it to the recommendation.

[16:12] SURESH IYER: Can I ask a different question? Why did the revision
not catch new SKUs?

[16:13] RAHUL SHARMA: Because the revision was applied as a remap of
existing SKUs. New SKUs created afterwards inherit the category default,
which was never updated.

[16:13] SURESH IYER: So the next revision will have the same problem.

[16:14] RAHUL SHARMA: Yes, unless the remap includes a completeness check
for subsequently created listings. I'd expect that to be raised as a
preventive action.

[16:14] ADITYA VERMA: Noted. I'll make sure it's an action rather than a
comment. Suresh, anything else?

[16:13] SURESH IYER: So the next revision will have the same problem.

[16:14] RAHUL SHARMA: Yes, unless the remap includes a completeness check
for subsequently created listings. I'd expect that to be raised as a
preventive action.

[16:14] ADITYA VERMA: Noted. I'll make sure it's an action rather than a
comment. Suresh, anything else?

[16:15] SURESH IYER: One thing. Please don't communicate this to us as
'system error' with no detail. My accountant will ask me what happened and
if I say system error he'll ask me again next year. Tell me the actual cause
in writing and I'll pass it on.

[16:15] ADITYA VERMA: That's reasonable. I'll ask for a short written
explanation you can hand over.

[16:16] SURESH IYER: Thank you. That's all I need.

[16:16] ADITYA VERMA: I'll come back to you by the twenty-eighth with either
approval or a problem.

[16:17] SURESH IYER: Understood. Thank you, Aditya. Rahul, thank you for
the quick confirmation.

[16:17] RAHUL SHARMA: No problem. I'll keep the ticket open until you
confirm your filing position is restored.

================================================================================
DECISIONS
================================================================================
1. Credit notes to be issued against the 1,240 incorrect invoices and
invoices re-issued at the correct rate. A net adjustment was rejected by
the seller and accepted as inappropriate by Business.
2. Platform absorbs the INR 2,17,600 difference.
3. A blocking validation to prevent publication of listings whose tax
category resolves to a default is to be added.
4. A written cause explanation suitable for the seller's auditor to be
provided.

FOLLOW-UP ACTIONS
================================================================================
Owner Action Target
Aditya Verma Obtain approval for absorbing the difference 2026-02-28
Operations Issue credit notes and re-issue invoices 2026-03-05
Engineering Deploy blocking tax mapping validation 2026-03-18
Support Provide written cause explanation 2026-03-02
Rahul Sharma Confirm seller filing position restored 2026-03-09
Aditya Verma Raise remap completeness check as an action 2026-03-20

correct me if I'm overstating.

[10:35] SURESH IYER: Can it happen again on the next cycle?

[10:34] RAHUL SHARMA: That's right. I don't have the technical detail yet,

[10:35] SURESH IYER: Can it happen again on the next cycle?

[10:35] RAHUL SHARMA: I can't rule it out until the fix is deployed. What I

[10:36] SURESH IYER: On hold is better than wrong. How long?

[10:36] RAHUL SHARMA: The fix is being developed today. If it deploys this

[10:37] SURESH IYER: And if it doesn't deploy?

[10:37] RAHUL SHARMA: Then I'll tell you by 18:00 today that it hasn't, and

[10:38] ADITYA VERMA: That's the commitment. Suresh, one question from me.
When you found this, what made you check the reversal block specifically?

[10:39] SURESH IYER: Because it's the only block I can't verify from my own
data. GMV I can check against orders. Commission I can check against the
contract. Reversals depend on your return processing, and I only see the
total. So it's the block I watch most closely.

[10:40] ADITYA VERMA: That's a really useful observation. If reversals are
the hardest thing for you to verify, then a per-return breakdown would help.

[10:40] SURESH IYER: Enormously. If I'd had line-level reversals I would
have caught this on the first day, not the fourth.

[10:41] ADITYA VERMA: Noted. I'm going to take that away. There's a project
already running on settlement controls and I think your point belongs in it.

[10:42] RITIKA BANSAL: Can I raise something else while we're all here?

[10:42] ADITYA VERMA: Please.

[10:43] RITIKA BANSAL: The detection. Suresh found this. Not you. We are the
control here. I've said this before and I'll keep saying it - I don't want to
be the mechanism that catches your accounting errors.

[10:44] ADITYA VERMA: You're right, and I'm not going to defend it. There is
no automated settlement check on our side. That's the actual gap, separate
from the bug.

[10:44] RITIKA BANSAL: Then that's what I want fixed.

[10:45] ADITYA VERMA: Agreed. I'll make sure it's an action with an owner
rather than a nice sentiment. Let me summarise where we are.

[10:46] ADITYA VERMA: One - shortfall confirmed at INR 4,82,000, cause is
ours, credit will be issued. Two - the payout is held so nothing incorrect
goes out. Three - Rahul gives you a status by 18:00 today either way. Four -
I'm taking forward two requests from this call: line-level reversal detail
in the settlement report, and an automated variance check before payout.

[10:48] SURESH IYER: Thank you.

[10:48] RITIKA BANSAL: One more thing, and then I'll let you go. What

================================================================================

3. Credit to be issued as a distinct adjustment line, not netted.
4. Support to provide a status update by 18:00 IST on 13 March either way.

[10:00] NEHA GUPTA: Thanks for joining at short notice. Before we go through
the remediation, I want to acknowledge the sequence: you reported a problem
yesterday morning, it was real, and it should not have reached you before we
saw it. I'm not going to dress that up.

[10:01] SAMEER KHANNA: I appreciate that, but let's not spend too long on it.
I want to know two things. Why did it happen, and can it happen again. Farah
has the data side.

[10:01] NEHA GUPTA: Vikram, cause first.

[10:02] VIKRAM SINGH: There were two problems acting together, which is
unusual and part of why it was hard to see. The first is that the scheduler
that picks your stock file was using a fixed offset instead of resolving the
Indian timezone. Your file arrives around eleven at night and the job runs at
two in the morning. With the wrong offset it selected the window from the
previous night.

[10:03] FARAH QURESHI: So it was processing yesterday's file.

[10:03] VIKRAM SINGH: Yes. That alone is about twenty-four hours of
staleness. The second problem is that an old SKU mapping table from the March
catalogue restructure was still in the pipeline as a fallback. Rows that
didn't match the new catalogue were silently resolved against the old table,
which pointed at identifiers that had changed.

[10:04] SAMEER KHANNA: Which is why the pattern was uneven.

[10:04] VIKRAM SINGH: Exactly. The timezone problem made everything stale.
The mapping problem made some SKUs wrong and dropped others entirely, which
is why your Chennai centre showed a different picture.

[10:05] FARAH QURESHI: We noticed that and couldn't explain it. That's
actually reassuring.

[10:05] SAMEER KHANNA: How did neither of these show in your monitoring?

[10:06] VIKRAM SINGH: Because the job reported success both times. It ran.
It processed a file. It published it. Nothing in the monitoring asked
whether the data was current.

No service was unavailable at any point. This was a correctness failure, not an availability failure, which is why no monitoring alert fired.
7. Investigation
The investigation followed three questions.
Was the returns data correct? Yes. The order and returns services showed 1,914 returns for the period,
matching the seller's own export exactly. The input was never in question.
Why were there two entries per return? Each pair had distinct entry identifiers and identical business content. Creation timestamps clustered in two groups, at 15:51 and at 16:22 on 11 March, which mapped to the original run and the retry.
Why did the retry not deduplicate? The ledger writes entries through an idempotent upsert keyed on a composite deduplication key. Inspecting the key construction in the v1.9 schema showed:
dedupe_key = hash(settlement_cycle_id, seller_id, entry_type)
For a sale entry this is sufficient, because a cycle produces one aggregate sale entry per seller. For a reversal entry it is not: a cycle can contain many reversals for one seller, all sharing cycle, seller and entry type. The key therefore could not distinguish one reversal from another.
The v1.8 key had been:
dedupe_key = hash(settlement_cycle_id, seller_id, entry_type, order_id)
The order_id component was dropped during the v1.8 to v1.9 migration. The migration changed the key to accommodate a new aggregate entry type that has no order identifier. The author made the field optional in the schema and removed it from the key rather than making the key type-dependent.
Because the upsert matched nothing on the retry, it inserted rather than updated.
8. Root Cause
The deduplication key for settlement ledger entries omitted order_id after the v1.8 to v1.9 schema migration. For reversal entries, which are order-scoped, this made the key non-unique. When the 5-9 March batch was reprocessed after a transient failure, every reversal entry was inserted a second time instead of being recognised as already present, double-deducting 1,914 returns and reducing the payout by INR
4,82,000.
Page 3 of 5

9. Contributing Factors
1. Reprocessing was not idempotent in practice. The design assumed idempotency from the deduplication key alone, with no independent safeguard against a batch being processed twice.
2. The migration was not tested against a reprocessing path. Test coverage exercised first-run behaviour for all entry types. No test reprocessed a batch containing reversals.
3. No settlement variance monitoring existed. A payout differing from order and return history by 4.5 percent produced no alert.
4. A schema change altered financial correctness without financial review.
The migration was reviewed as a schema change. Its effect on ledger uniqueness guarantees was not examined.
5. A successful job log masked an incorrect outcome. Both runs reported success, because both did what they were asked to do.
10. Mitigation
Immediate mitigation was to hold the payout for the cycle at 16:00 on 12 March, once duplication was confirmed but before the corrected figure was known. This prevented the incorrect amount from being treated as final while the investigation continued.
No traffic shifting or rollback was applicable. The defect was in data already written, not in a running request path.
11. Resolution
The deduplication key was restored to include the order identifier, with a type-dependent construction so that aggregate entry types without an order identifier remain valid:
 For order-scoped entry types: `hash(cycle_id, seller_id, entry_type,
order_id)`.
 For aggregate entry types: hash(cycle_id, seller_id, entry_type).
The duplicate entries for the affected batch were removed and the batch was reprocessed under an explicit replay token. The corrected payout was verified by Operations against the Payment Recovery Runbook
(OPS-RB-004), and the shortfall of INR 4,82,000 was credited on 14 March 2026. The controlling rule is the uniqueness requirement for ledger entries under the Payment and Settlement Policy (POL-FIN-002).

13.1 On PA-2 and PA-4
PA-2 introduces three invariants checked before any payout is authorised: every reversal entry maps to exactly one originating order line, entry types sum to the batch net, and no entry appears more than once under its composite key. The third invariant is the one that would have caught this incident.
PA-4 removes the trigger condition entirely. A batch now carries a processing token and a second run with the same token is rejected unless an operator explicitly authorises a replay with a documented reason.
Correctness no longer depends solely on the deduplication key being right.
14. Follow-Up
The broader finding from this incident was not the key defect. It was that the platform had no way to know a settlement was wrong until a seller reconciled it manually. That finding opened the settlement reconciliation hardening project (PRJ-S001-SRH), which tracks PA-2, PA-3 and PA-4 along with a seller-facing variance statement.
Post-incident review held 16 March 2026 with Engineering, Operations, Support and Business. The review accepted the root cause without dispute and concentrated on detection rather than on the defect itself.

Release 4.12.0 introduced a cache key change intended to support multi-region cart replication. The key gained a region prefix:

With nine of twelve instances upgraded, the probability of a cross-version pair on any given checkout was approximately 37 percent, and roughly one in five of those produced a user-visible failure after internal retries. This matches the observed 7.2 percent peak.
Testing had not caught it because the staging environment deploys all instances simultaneously. There is no mixed-version state in staging, so the only failing combinations never occurred.
8. Root Cause
Release 4.12.0 changed the cart token cache key format to include a region prefix but did not change the corresponding signing key namespace derivation. During the rolling deployment, instances on 4.11.7 and
4.12.0 issued and validated tokens under incompatible key schemes, causing validation failures for any checkout whose requests crossed versions.
Page 3 of 5

9. Contributing Factors
1. No mixed-version testing. Staging deploys atomically and cannot reproduce a rolling deployment state.
2. No compatibility guard. Nothing in the release prevented a token format change from being deployed without a transition period.
3. Alert threshold tuned for outages. A drop from 98.9 to 91.7 percent success was invisible to an alert set at 85 percent.
4. Token validation failures were not logged as errors. The service treated them as normal business outcomes, so error dashboards were clean throughout.
5. The change description understated the risk. The release note described the change as adding multi-region cache support. It did not identify a change to a cross-instance data contract.
10. Mitigation
The deployment was halted at 11:58 and rolled back to 4.11.7 starting at 12:02, following the Deployment
Rollback Procedure. Rollback completed at 12:36. Failure rate returned to baseline within four minutes of the last instance reverting.
Rollback was chosen over rolling forward because the fix was not yet understood at 12:02 and the failure mode was known to disappear once the fleet was homogeneous.
Time from escalation to mitigation: 52 minutes.
11. Resolution
Release 4.12.1 was built with three changes:
1. Signing key namespace derivation updated to match the new cache key format.
2. A dual-read transition: 4.12.1 validates tokens under both the prefixed and unprefixed schemes, so a mixed fleet is tolerated during any future rolling deployment of this change.
3. An explicit token format version embedded in the token itself, so a validating instance can determine which scheme applies rather than inferring it.
4.12.1 was deployed on 13 August at 16:00 with no failures observed.

7. Investigation
7.1 How The Credential Escaped
The credential originated in a diagnostic script written by a support engineer to troubleshoot a feed delivery problem on this account. At that time Support had no central diagnostic tooling for seller feeds, so engineers assembled ad hoc scripts, and those scripts contained connection details because there was no credential-resolution mechanism available to them.
The script was later shared externally as part of a technical discussion about SFTP transfer behaviour. The person sharing it believed the credential was a staging credential and therefore harmless.
It was labelled staging. It was not: the S002 integration used the same credential for its staging and production directories, a configuration dating from the 2022 onboarding that had never been reviewed.

The conclusion was that the credential was validated by an attacker but not used, or that use was attempted and failed for another reason. The absence of evidence of access was recorded as exactly that, not as evidence of absence.
7.3 Why Rotation Was Not Automatic
Credential rotation for seller service accounts was a manual process requiring a scheduled coordination window with the seller. In practice this meant rotation happened rarely. The exposed credential had been in use unchanged since June 2022, approximately 46 months.
8. Root Cause
A valid production SFTP credential for seller S002 was embedded in a support diagnostic script and shared outside the company. The exposure was possible because Support had no central diagnostic tooling that resolved credentials at runtime, because the account used a single credential for both staging and production directories, because credential rotation was manual and had not occurred in 46 months, and because no secret scanning existed in the CI pipeline to detect credentials in code.
9. Contributing Factors
1. No secret scanning in the CI pipeline or in code review.
2. Shared staging and production credential on this account, so a credential believed to be low-risk was in fact production-scoped.
3. Manual rotation with a coordination burden that discouraged it.
4. No IP allowlisting on the endpoint, so a valid credential from any source address would have authenticated.
5. No central support tooling, forcing engineers to handle raw credentials.
6. No periodic access review of long-lived service credentials.
10. Containment
The containment decision was to rotate immediately rather than to schedule a coordinated rotation with the seller. This deliberately broke the seller's feeds for 80 minutes.
Page 4 of 6

The reasoning was proportionality. An 80-minute feed interruption is recoverable: files queue and are processed on resumption, and no orders or customer transactions depend on the feed within that window. A
compromised credential with write access to a catalogue and price feed is not recoverable in the same sense, because ingested price data affects live listings immediately.
The seller accepted this without objection once the reasoning was explained.

7. Investigation
7.1 The Scheduler Fault
The batch selects a stock window relative to the run time. The window calculation used a fixed UTC offset constant rather than resolving Asia/Kolkata.
BluePeak delivers its stock file at approximately 23:00 IST. The job runs at 02:00 IST. Under correct behaviour the job selects the window ending at the most recent file delivery. Under the fixed-offset calculation the window boundary fell 5 hours 30 minutes earlier, before the file was delivered, so the job selected the previous night's file.
This alone produced roughly 24 hours of staleness.
7.2 The Mapping Fault
The March 2026 catalogue restructure introduced new catalogue identifiers. A migration mapped old seller
SKUs to new identifiers and wrote a new mapping table. The legacy table was retained as a fallback for rows that failed to resolve against the new table, and the fallback was never removed.
Rows failing to resolve against the current mapping silently resolved against the legacy table. Where the legacy mapping pointed at a catalogue identifier that had since been reassigned, stock was published against the wrong SKU. Where the legacy mapping pointed at an identifier that no longer existed, the row was dropped without report.
This explains the uneven distribution and the missing SKUs, and added up to a further two hours of apparent staleness where stock landed on the wrong identifier.
7.3 Why Neither Alone Was Sufficient
The freshness requirement is six hours. The scheduler fault alone produced about 24 hours of staleness,
which would have breached the requirement had anything been measuring it. Nothing was. The mapping fault alone produced incorrect rather than stale data, which would have surfaced as individual SKU
complaints rather than as a systemic pattern.
Together they produced a large, visible, systemic failure that the seller detected within days. Paradoxically,
the combination is what made the problem detectable at all.
8. Root Cause
The nightly stock batch published stale and partially misdirected inventory because the scheduler computed its window using a fixed UTC offset rather than the Asia/Kolkata timezone, causing it to process the previous
Page 3 of 5

night's file, and because a legacy SKU mapping table retained as a silent fallback resolved rows that should have been rejected.
9. Contributing Factors
1. No freshness metric. The pipeline measured completion, not currency.
2. A silent fallback. The legacy mapping made a failure look like a success. A strict rejection would have surfaced the problem in March.
3. Implicit timezone handling. The scheduler relied on a constant rather than an explicit timezone, a pattern not specific to this job.
4. Migration cleanup incomplete. The March restructure left a fallback in place with no removal date or owner.
5. Requirement not enforced. The six-hour freshness requirement existed in the integration specification but had no corresponding control.
10. Mitigation
The effective mitigation was the seller disabling affected listings at 10:35 on 19 May, which stopped new oversells within about 20 minutes. This was the seller's decision, taken on a call with Support, and it was the right one: continuing to trade on unreliable availability would have compounded the harm for the 24 hours needed to correct the pipeline.
No platform-side mitigation was available that would have been faster. The correct stock position could not be published until the pipeline was fixed.

7. Investigation
7.1 The Proximate Cause
Order placement calls the inventory lookup service synchronously. Under normal load that call returns in about 40 ms. Under flash-sale load it slowed to 600-900 ms, because the lookup fans out across a much larger set of SKUs than a typical order.
Each in-flight placement holds a connection from a fixed pool of 120 for the duration of that call. At 9x baseline traffic with a 15x slower dependency, demand for connections exceeded 120 within about four minutes. Once the pool was full, new requests queued with no acquisition timeout and eventually returned
503.
7.2 The Amplification
The failure would have been self-limiting if clients had backed off. They did not.
BluePeak's client retried timed-out placements without limit and without backoff. Every 503 produced another request. Measured inbound volume at 20:18 was approximately 3.4 times the volume implied by actual buyer activity, so roughly 70 percent of the traffic at peak was retries of already-failed requests.
This is why no static capacity figure would have been sufficient. An unbounded retry loop expands to consume whatever capacity exists.
7.3 The Missing Control
The inventory lookup had no circuit breaker. A slow dependency should eventually be bypassed or failed fast, so that callers release their connections. Instead, every caller waited the full timeout, and the timeout on that path was 10 seconds.
A 10-second timeout with a 120-connection pool caps throughput at 12 requests per second once the dependency is slow, regardless of how much capacity the service otherwise has.
8. Root Cause
The order service connection pool was exhausted because synchronous inventory lookups slowed under flash-sale load and were not protected by a circuit breaker or an acquisition timeout, while an unbounded client retry policy amplified inbound traffic to roughly 3.4 times genuine demand. The combination converted a capacity pressure into a 40-minute cascading failure.
9. Contributing Factors
Page 3 of 5

1. No circuit breaker on a synchronous dependency in the critical path.
2. No connection acquisition timeout, so requests queued instead of failing fast.
3. Unbounded client retries at the seller, with no backoff or jitter.
4. HTTP 503 as the overload response, which does not communicate a retry strategy. A 429 with Retry-After states the correct behaviour explicitly.
5. No advance notice of the sale. The platform learned of the event when the traffic arrived. No capacity assessment was possible.
6. Pool sized for steady state, never load-tested against a dependency degradation scenario.
10. Mitigation
Two actions restored service.
The emergency pool increase from 120 to 240 at 20:26 bought immediate headroom and reduced the error rate from 31 percent to approximately 10 percent within 12 minutes. This treated the symptom.
Rate limiting the highest-volume client at 20:31 addressed the amplification and took the error rate below 2
percent by 20:44. This was the action that actually ended the incident, and it is uncomfortable: the platform throttled a seller's traffic during that seller's own revenue event. It was the correct call, because the throttled traffic was overwhelmingly retries rather than genuine buyer demand.
Time from escalation to mitigation: 32 minutes.
11. Resolution
Permanent remediation was delivered under the S002 throughput and resilience programme, workstream
WS-A, on 26 August 2026:
 Circuit breaker on the inventory lookup, opening at a 25 percent error rate over a 10-second window with a 30-second half-open probe.
 Connection pool resized to 300 with an explicit acquisition timeout of
750 ms, so a saturated pool fails fast.
 Request-level timeout of 2.5 seconds on the order placement path, replacing
10 seconds.
 Overload responses changed from HTTP 503 to HTTP 429 with Retry-After.
BluePeak owns the client-side changes: bounded retries with exponential backoff and jitter, honouring
Retry-After, and a client-side circuit breaker. Those are scheduled in the seller's October release train.

7. Investigation
7.1 Why Failover Did Not Happen
The failover logic is threshold-based: when the primary provider's error rate exceeds 40 percent over a two-minute window, the service switches to the backup. That threshold was breached at 06:10 and the switch was attempted.
The backup provider requires an OAuth client credential exchange before label requests can be made. The stored client secret for RapidPost had an expiry date of 31 May 2026 and had not been renewed. The token exchange returned a 401.
The failover handler treated any exception during provider initialisation as a transient failure of that provider and reverted to the previously selected provider, which was the degraded primary. It logged the reversion at debug level.
So the service made a correct decision to fail over, discovered it could not, and then made the worst available choice silently.
7.2 Why The Expiry Was Not Noticed
The credential store recorded the expiry date. Nothing monitored it. There was no report, alert or dashboard covering credential expiry for provider integrations.
The backup provider had never been used in production. It was configured in October 2025 as open item
OI-1 from the seller's onboarding project, and that item was closed on the evidence of a configuration entry rather than a successful failover test. In the eight months between configuration and this incident, no label had ever been generated through RapidPost in production.
An expired credential on a path that is never exercised is indistinguishable from a working configuration.
7.3 Why Falling Back Was Worse Than Failing
Had the service stopped and reported a terminal error at 06:10, the seller would have known within minutes rather than forty. The dark store teams could have held the pick, or the operations team could have arranged a manual dispatch for the highest-value baskets.
Page 3 of 6

Instead the service continued retrying, producing exactly the signals a healthy-but-slow system produces.
Everyone who looked at it, including the on-call engineer who acknowledged the 05:58 alert, saw a system responding to a known provider problem.
8. Root Cause
Automatic failover to the backup courier provider did not activate because the stored backup credentials had expired, and the failover path validated credentials only at the moment failover was attempted. The failover handler treated the resulting authentication failure as a transient provider error and silently reverted to the degraded primary provider, so label generation remained unavailable and no failure was surfaced.
9. Contributing Factors
1. Failover path never exercised in production in eight months of configuration.
2. No credential expiry monitoring for provider integrations.
3. Silent reversion on failover failure, logged at debug level.
4. Onboarding item closed on configuration evidence rather than on a successful test.
5. Alert acknowledged on an assumption that failover would handle a known provider degradation.
6. No end-to-end label generation health check independent of provider selection.
10. Mitigation
Credentials were rotated with the backup provider at 08:05 and failover was executed manually at 08:20.
Labels began generating immediately and the backlog of 2,100 cleared by 09:15.
There was no faster mitigation available. The primary provider remained degraded until approximately 11:00,
so the backup was the only viable path, and the backup could not be used until its credentials were valid.
Time from escalation to mitigation: 68 minutes, of which 23 minutes were spent identifying that failover had not occurred and 30 minutes obtaining rotated credentials from the provider.

No component malfunctioned. Every component did exactly what it was built to do. The defect was an incorrect assumption about delivery semantics.
7. Investigation
7.1 The Mechanism
The event broker provides at-least-once delivery. A consumer receives an event, processes it, and acknowledges. If the consumer terminates after processing but before acknowledging, the broker redelivers on restart.
The deployment at 21:12 on 2 September performed a rolling restart. Consumer instances were terminated with a 30-second grace period. Events that had been processed within that window but not yet acknowledged were redelivered when the replacement instances started.
The consumer's refund application logic was:
1. Receive refund event.
2. Look up the order and the original payment.
3. Issue a refund to the payment processor.
4. Record the refund locally.
5. Acknowledge the event.
There is no step that asks whether this refund event has already been applied. A redelivered event therefore produced a second, entirely valid, refund transaction.
7.2 Why 640 And Not More
The redelivery window was bounded by the number of events in flight at restart. 640 events had been processed and not acknowledged across the consumer group at the moment of the rolling restart, which is consistent with the account's refund volume and the 30-second grace period.
The five-hour tail between 21:15 and 02:40 reflects the redelivery backlog being worked through alongside ongoing live traffic, not a five-hour window of new duplication.
7.3 Why This Was Not Caught Earlier
The consumer was written in 2023, before at-least-once handling was an explicit written requirement. The requirement now exists in two places: as ORD-3 in the S002 integration specification and as a design decision in the S001 order webhook receiver, which deduplicates on order identifier.
Page 3 of 6

Both of those were written for order events. Nobody revisited the refund consumer against the same requirement. It had also never been restarted under load in a way that produced a meaningful redelivery volume, so the defect had no opportunity to surface.
8. Root Cause
The refund webhook consumer applied refund events without checking whether an event had already been processed. Because the event broker provides at-least-once delivery, a rolling restart during a deployment caused 640 processed-but-unacknowledged events to be redelivered and applied a second time, issuing duplicate refunds totalling INR 1,18,000 in excess.
9. Contributing Factors
1. No idempotency check on a financial operation consuming an at-least-once stream.
2. Requirement not applied consistently. At-least-once handling was required for order events and never audited across other consumers.
3. No refund volume monitoring per account against expected volume.
4. Grace period shorter than the acknowledgement path, making redelivery likely on any rolling restart.
5. Deployment performed during the account's peak refund window, evening being when quality reports are raised.
6. Duplicate refunds are silent. Each one succeeds; nothing fails.
10. Mitigation
The idempotency store was deployed at 16:30 on 4 September, which stopped any further duplication.
Before that, no mitigation was applied: the duplication had already ended at 02:40 when the redelivery backlog cleared, so there was no ongoing harm to stop.
The substantive mitigation question was financial rather than technical, and it belonged to Operations: how to recover INR 1,18,000 from a cash- constrained seller who had not caused the error.
The decision was to recover across four settlement cycles beginning 15 September, with no interest or fee.
Customers who received a duplicate refund were not asked to return it. Both the idempotency requirement and the staged recovery default are set by the Payment and Settlement Policy (POL-FIN-002) and executed under the Payment Recovery Runbook (OPS-RB-004).

StrideOne's marketplace lead raised a ticket on 5 August reporting a return rate rise from 9 to 27 percent over three weeks, with 'size too small' having grown from 14 percent to 71 percent of return reasons, across all four logistics partners and all product lines, with no change on the seller's side.
Support sampled twenty SKUs across four brands within hours and found that brands supplying UK sizing were published approximately two sizes small while a brand supplying EU sizing was correct. That sampling produced the double-conversion hypothesis before the ticket reached Engineering.
No platform control detected this. There was no validation comparing published size distribution against source, and no alert on a return reason code shifting from 14 percent to 71 percent of volume.

7. Investigation
7.1 The Defect
Before 14 July, size normalisation was a single step: read the partner's declared size and its convention,
then convert to the published EU convention.
The 14 July schema update introduced a normalised_size field to the partner staging record, intended to hold the converted value so that downstream steps would not need the conversion table. The update added the conversion at the staging write step.
The publication step was not changed. It continued to read the size field and apply the conversion before publishing.
After the update, the staging record already held a converted value, and the publication step converted it again. A UK 8 became EU 42 at staging, then EU 42 was treated as a UK value and converted again to approximately EU 47 in internal units, which after the chart mapping presented to buyers as a shoe roughly two sizes smaller than reality for the size label shown.
Partners supplying EU sizing were unaffected, because the conversion is a no-op for values already in the target convention.
7.2 Why Testing Did Not Catch It
The change was tested with unit tests on the new staging write step, which correctly produced a converted value, and with an end-to-end import test using a fixture file. The fixture used EU sizing, because it had been created from a partner sample that happened to be EU-based.
The end-to-end test therefore exercised the only path where double conversion is invisible.
7.3 Why This Class Of Defect Is Hard
The onboarding project for this account recorded a design note in August 2025 that turned out to be exactly right:
Page 3 of 6

"Size conversion is the only transformation in this feed that cannot be validated by inspecting a single record.
A wrong colour is obvious; a wrong size is only detectable by comparing the published chart against the physical product or against return data. Validation must therefore be structural rather than per-record."
The structural validation that note called for was recorded as open item OI-2 with a target of January 2026. It was not implemented. It was delivered on 19 August 2026, seven months late and five days after this defect was confirmed.
8. Root Cause
A schema update to the dropship feed importer on 14 July 2026 added size conversion at the staging write step without removing the existing conversion at the publication step. Sizes supplied in UK convention were therefore converted twice, publishing size charts approximately two sizes smaller than the physical product for approximately 13,400 SKUs.
9. Contributing Factors
1. Conversion added without removing the existing conversion, a transformation applied at two layers.
2. Test fixture used EU sizing, the one convention for which the defect is invisible.
3. No structural validation of published size distribution against source,
despite a design note requiring it and an open item tracking it.
4. Open item OI-2 carried for seven months without escalation.
5. No alert on return reason code distribution, the only available signal.
6. The seller cannot inspect goods. In a dropship model no one in the chain physically checks the product against its listing.
10. Mitigation
There was no fast mitigation. Correcting the conversion on 12 August fixed future imports, but the incorrect size charts remained published until the catalogue was fully republished on 19 August.
A rollback of the 14 July schema update was considered and rejected. The update had other dependencies that had accumulated over four weeks, and rolling back would have reintroduced a different set of defects.
Correcting forward was the lower-risk path.
In-flight returns continued for a further two weeks after republication, because customers who had already received wrongly sized goods returned them on their own timescale. The return rate therefore lagged the fix by approximately three weeks, which is precisely what later triggered the automated suspension.

Two follow-ups extend beyond this incident.
The first is SC-012. The automated suspension on 8 September was triggered by a trailing 30-day return rate that was still elevated by this defect. The risk rule is being recalibrated to exclude return volume attributable to a recorded platform defect and to incorporate a trend component.
The second is PA-6. The conversion exists only because partners supply sizes in three conventions.
Requiring a single convention in the 2027 partner contracts would remove the transformation, and therefore this entire class of defect, rather than validating around it.
Post-incident review held 22 August 2026. The review's principal finding was not the coding error but the seven-month-old open item: the control that would have prevented this was identified at onboarding, agreed,

from signed commercial agreement through to handover to account management. It is the operational counterpart to the Seller Onboarding Policy: the policy states what must be true, this runbook states who does what and in what order.
2. Scope
Applies to every new seller account regardless of tier, category or integration method. Applies also to a material change of integration method on an existing account, for example a move from batch to real-time integration.
Does not apply to tier changes, commercial term changes or catalogue expansion on an already-onboarded account.

5. Procedure
Stage 1 - Account Setup
1. Create the seller account record with seller ID, registered name,
category and tier.
2. Apply the agreed commission mapping. Use sub-category mapping where margin varies materially across the range rather than a single flat rate.
3. Configure the settlement cycle and payout lag for the tier.
4. Record any category exception explicitly against the account. Do not hold category exceptions as informal knowledge.
5. Assign the account manager, support owner and operations owner.
Recording category exceptions against the account is not optional. A refund-on-report exception for perishable goods, for example, changes how refund volume should be interpreted for that account and must be findable by anyone investigating a refund anomaly later.
Stage 2 - Credential and Access Provisioning
1. Raise a credential request with IT for the selected integration method.
2. Issue separate credentials for staging and production. Never a shared credential across environments.
3. Configure IP allowlisting where the integration method supports it.
4. Confirm the credential is enrolled in automated rotation.
5. Record credential ownership and expiry in the credential store.
Stage 3 - Integration Enablement
1. Provision sandbox access and confirm the seller can authenticate.
2. Walk the seller counterpart through the relevant API or feed contract.
3. Agree the data quality rules that will apply and how rejections are reported.
4. For batch integrations, confirm the delivery schedule and pin all scheduled jobs to an explicit timezone.
5. For real-time integrations, confirm that the seller's consumer tolerates at-least-once delivery and deduplicates appropriately.

Stage 4 - Catalogue Preparation
1. Run a test catalogue load in sandbox.
2. Review the validation error report with the seller.
3. Correct or withhold failing records. **Withholding a record is preferable to publishing it with poor data.**
4. Confirm tax category mapping resolves explicitly for every listing. A
listing whose tax category resolves to a category default must be held for classification.
Stage 5 - Fulfilment Verification
1. Verify each fulfilment node or logistics partner.
2. Assess dispatch capacity and record the surge figure.
3. Configure label generation with a primary and a backup provider.
4. Execute a live failover test. Disable the primary provider and confirm that a label is generated through the backup.
5. Record any single point of failure explicitly, with the seller's acknowledgement.
Stage 6 - Pilot
1. Run a limited pilot with a bounded customer or order volume.
2. Verify order intake, dispatch, settlement and return flows end to end.
3. Record every defect found, including those fixed during the pilot.
4. Do not treat a pilot with no findings as a success. It usually means the pilot was too small or too narrow.
Stage 7 - Go-Live
1. Confirm all preconditions and stage exits.
2. Confirm Support queue readiness and brief the support owner.
3. Activate the account.
4. Monitor order flow, dispatch performance and the first settlement cycle.
Stage 8 - Stabilisation Review and Closure
1. Hold a review two weeks after go-live.
2. Assess order flow, dispatch SLA, first settlement reconciliation and ticket volume.
3. List open items with an owner and a target date for each.
4. Hand over to Business.

1. Purpose
This procedure defines how Operations restores correct service and correct data after a platform failure. It covers the period after the immediate technical cause has been addressed by Engineering and before the incident can be closed.
The distinction it enforces is the reason it exists: a service returning to health is not the same as the data it produced being correct. Most of the recovery work on this platform is data recovery, not service restart.
2. Scope
Applies to any incident where a platform service produced incorrect, stale, duplicated or missing data, or where a business process was interrupted.
Applies to feed pipelines, event consumers, settlement computation, fulfilment integrations and catalogue publication.
Does not cover deployment rollback, which is OPS-RB-005, or escalation routing, which is OPS-RB-003.
3. Preconditions
1. An incident is open with an identified Engineering owner.
2. The immediate cause has been mitigated, or a mitigation plan is agreed.
3. The affected data domain and time window are known, at least approximately.
4. An Operations recovery owner has been named.
Do not begin data recovery while the cause is still active. Recovering data into a system that is still producing bad data wastes the effort and obscures the boundary of the problem.
4. Responsibilities

5. Procedure
Page 1 of 5

Step 1 - Establish the Blast Radius
Before recovering anything, determine the boundary.
1. Identify the time window: first and last affected record.
2. Identify the data domain: which entities are wrong, and in what way.
3. Identify the affected accounts, and whether the pattern is platform-wide or account-specific.
4. Quantify. A count of affected records is required, not an estimate.
Where the start of the window cannot be established, record that explicitly and use the earliest evidenced point. An undetermined start is itself a finding and belongs in the incident report.
Step 2 - Classify the Data Fault
Fault type
Recovery approach
Stale data
Resynchronise from source after correcting the pipeline
Duplicated data
Identify duplicates by a business key, reverse the surplus
Missing data
Replay from the source or the event log
Incorrect transformation
Correct the logic, then republish the affected population
Unprocessed backlog
Process the backlog, then verify no gap remains
Classification determines the approach and the verification method. Do not begin execution until the fault type is agreed with the Engineering owner.
Step 3 - Decide Whether to Halt the Flow
Ask whether continuing to operate causes further harm.
Halt where continued operation creates irreversible harm: accepting orders against stock known to be wrong,
dispatching against an incorrect catalogue, or paying out from a ledger known to be incorrect.
Do not halt where the harm is reporting lag or internal inconvenience and the flow can be corrected in place.
In May 2026 a seller disabled affected listings roughly twenty minutes after stale-stock oversells were confirmed. That decision stopped further oversells for the twenty-four hours needed to correct the pipeline.
Halting was correct because an oversell cannot be unwound: the customer has paid for something that does not exist.
Step 4 - Build the Recovery Plan
The plan must state:
1. The recovery approach per Step 2.
2. The order of operations, with dependencies.
3. Whether a replay authorisation is required, and from whom.
4. The verification method and the acceptance threshold.
5. The rollback position if recovery makes matters worse.
6. The seller communication points.
Record the plan before executing it. A recovery executed from memory cannot be verified.
Step 5 - Execute
Page 2 of 5

1. Correct the source of the fault first. Confirm with Engineering.
2. Where reprocessing is required, obtain explicit replay authorisation. A
batch carrying a processing token must not be rerun under the same token without a documented reason.
3. Execute in the smallest safe increment. Verify the increment before proceeding.
4. Preserve the incorrect data until verification is complete. Do not delete evidence during recovery.
Step 6 - Verify
Verification is against the source of truth, not against the system that failed.
Fault type
Verification

For transformation faults, per-record sampling is not sufficient. A transformation defect can leave every individual record plausible while shifting the whole population; compare distributions.
Step 7 - Remediate Affected Parties
1. Identify customers and sellers who bore a loss.
2. Refer commercial remediation to Business. Operations does not decide who absorbs a cost.
3. Where recovery requires money to be reclaimed from a seller, stage it across settlement cycles unless the seller requests otherwise. A single large debit on a cash-constrained account causes real harm for no benefit.
4. Where an amount is uneconomic to pursue, recommend write-off with a rationale.
Step 8 - Close
1. Confirm verification passed and record the evidence.
2. Confirm preventive actions are raised with owners and dates.
3. Confirm the seller has been told the outcome, not only the cause.
4. Sign off recovery and hand the incident back to the Engineering owner for report completion.

Its purpose is to remove judgement from routing and timing, so that the quality of an escalation does not depend on who happens to receive the report.

3.1 Severity Is Set By Harm, Not By Volume
A low record count can be SEV-1. 2,100 undispatched orders would be SEV-2 on most accounts; on a perishable account where a missed slot destroys the goods, it is SEV-1, because the harm is irreversible within the response window.
Conversely a high record count can be SEV-3. A nine-hour stale settlement feed affecting thousands of records was SEV-3 in June 2026 because no money had moved incorrectly and the cycle had not closed.

6. Procedure
Step 1 - Acknowledge and Classify

 When it started, or the earliest evidenced point.
 Whether it is account-specific or broader.
 What has been ruled out.
 A hypothesis, where one is available.
A support engineer who sampled twenty product records across four brands in August 2026 was able to escalate with a specific hypothesis - a size conversion applied twice - rather than a report of rising returns.
That sampling removed roughly a day from diagnosis.

Escalating severity mid-incident is normal and should not be treated as an admission of error. A return-rate data quality issue raised at SEV-3 in August 2026 was raised to SEV-1 two days later once the commercial scale and the proximity to an automated suspension threshold were understood.
Step 6 - Hand Off To Recovery
When the immediate cause is mitigated, hand off to the Service Recovery Procedure with a named
Operations recovery owner. Do not close an incident at mitigation. Service health is not data correctness.
7. Security Escalation
Security events follow a separate path with a shorter clock.
1. Any suspected credential exposure, unauthorised access or data exposure is
SEV-1 by default, regardless of confirmed impact.
2. Escalate to IT immediately. The Platform Administrator owns the incident.
3. The Platform Administrator may authorise immediate containment, including credential rotation, without seller consent and without waiting for seller readiness.
4. Classify the incident record RESTRICTED at creation. Do not discuss detail in CONFIDENTIAL or INTERNAL channels.
5. Treat an exposed credential as compromised. Absence of evidence of use is not evidence of non-use.
Containment that interrupts a seller's service is acceptable where the alternative risk is larger. Rotating a credential in April 2026 broke a seller's feeds for 80 minutes; the alternative was leaving write access to a
Page 3 of 4

price feed in the hands of an unknown party.
8. Account Risk Escalation
Automated account actions, including suspension, escalate to Operations as the policy owner, with Business notified within 30 minutes.
Where an automated action may have been triggered by a platform defect, establish that before defending the action. Pull the underlying metric as a trend, not as the trailing average the rule evaluated, and check for an open platform defect linked to the account.
9. Exceptions
A severity may be set lower than section 3 implies where a compensating control bounds the harm, the reasoning is recorded, and Business is informed.
An escalation timeframe may be missed only where the delay is recorded with a reason. A missed SEV-1
timeframe is itself reportable at the post-incident review.
10. Verification and Post-Incident Actions
1. Confirm the escalation timeframes that were met and missed.
2. Confirm whether detection was internal or by a seller. Seller detection is a detection gap and must be raised as a preventive action.
3. Confirm whether an alert existed, fired, and was assessed. An alert that fired and was acknowledged on an assumption is a process failure, not a monitoring success.
4. Record the final severity and whether it changed during the incident.

Financial recovery differs from other recovery in one respect that governs everything in this document:

1. Purpose
This procedure defines how a release is withdrawn from production when it is causing harm, and how the decision between rolling back and rolling forward is made.
2. Scope
Applies to any production release of a platform service. Applies to configuration changes deployed through the release pipeline. Applies to schema migrations, with the additional constraints in section 7.
Does not apply to emergency configuration changes applied outside the pipeline, which follow the Incident
Escalation Procedure.
3. Preconditions
1. An incident is open, or is opened as part of invoking this procedure.
2. The harm is observed in production, not suspected.
3. The release under suspicion is identified, with its deployment start time.
4. A named decision owner is present: the Engineering incident owner.
Correlation with a deployment time is sufficient to invoke this procedure. Confirmed causation is not required and waiting for it is usually the wrong choice.

This is the only significant decision in the procedure.

Default to rollback. Understanding a defect takes longer than reverting one, and a rollback returns the system to a known state. Roll forward only where rollback is unsafe or where the fix is genuinely trivial and understood.
In August 2026 a checkout release caused token validation failures. The cause was not understood at the point of decision, harm was accruing on a shared revenue path, and the failure mode was known to disappear once all instances ran the same version. Rollback was initiated 4 minutes after the decision point and completed in 34 minutes. Root cause was confirmed five hours later, comfortably after service was restored.
6. Procedure
Step 1 - Halt the Deployment
Stop the rollout before deciding anything else. A partially deployed release that is causing harm will cause more harm as it proceeds, and a mixed fleet is often the failure condition itself.
Step 2 - Decide
1. Apply section 5.
2. Record the decision and its reasoning in the incident record.
3. Name the executor.
Target: decision within 10 minutes of the deployment being halted.
Step 3 - Execute Rollback
1. Revert to the last known good version, instance by instance.
2. Monitor the harm metric continuously during reversion. It should improve proportionally as instances revert.
3. If the metric does not improve as instances revert, stop. The release is probably not the cause and reverting further adds risk without benefit.
4. Confirm the fleet is homogeneous at the reverted version.
Step 4 - Verify Service

Acceptance

At baseline
Fleet version consistency

Step 5 - Verify Data
A rollback restores code. It does not restore data written by the defective version.
1. Determine whether the defective version wrote incorrect data.
2. If it did, hand off to the Service Recovery Procedure with a named recovery owner.
3. Do not close the incident on service restoration alone.
Step 6 - Communicate
1. Confirm to Support that service is restored so that sellers can be told.
2. Where a seller reported the issue, confirm resolution against their original report rather than against internal metrics.
Step 7 - Corrected Release
The release owner produces the corrected version. It must include:
1. The fix for the defect.
2. A control that prevents the same class of defect. For a data contract change, this normally means a transition mechanism such as dual-read, or an explicit version field, rather than a one-way change.
3. Test coverage for the condition that was missed.
Re-release only after the corrected version has been validated against the specific failure condition, not merely against the normal path.
7. Schema Migrations
Schema migrations constrain rollback and require additional care.
1. A migration must be backward compatible with the previous application version for at least one release cycle.
2. A migration that cannot be reversed must be identified as such before deployment, and the release must be deployable and revertible independently of it.
3. Never combine an irreversible migration with an application change in the same deployment.
4. A migration that alters a uniqueness guarantee, a key, or a constraint on financial data requires financial review before deployment, not only engineering review.
Requirement 4 exists because a deduplication key change during a schema migration in early 2026 removed a uniqueness guarantee on settlement ledger reversal entries and produced an incorrect payout. The change was reviewed as a schema change; its effect on financial correctness was not examined.

Rule R-9 was added in July 2026. A failover condition had been closed in October 2025 on a configuration entry; when the failover was required eight months later, the stored credentials had expired and no label could be generated for 2,100 perishable orders. The condition had been recorded as met and had never been true.

R-11. An exception to any condition in sections 4 or 5 requires all of the following:
1. A written rationale stating what is being waived and why.
2. A named approver with authority for the affected domain.
3. A compensating control that bounds the resulting risk.
4. Milestones with named validators where the condition is deferred rather than waived.
5. An expiry date, after which the exception lapses and the entitlement is withdrawn.

R-13. Two-stage onboarding is permitted where an interim process is used at activation, provided the exception carries an explicit exit date. An open-ended commitment to migrate is not an acceptable exception; in practice it becomes permanent.
R-14. A compensating control must be proportionate to the exposure it bounds, and must be sized against the risk rather than against the seller's convenience. A security deposit, for example, is sized against the largest single-cycle dispute observed on comparable accounts.
R-15. Every active exception is reviewed at each quarterly account review.
7.1 Worked Example
A grocery seller requested a tier upgrade and weekly settlement in January 2026, having completed four settlement cycles, with no automated reconciliation and an untested failover.
The tier upgrade was granted immediately, because tier risk is commercially reversible. Weekly settlement was deferred and tied to validation of the reconciliation milestone, with a security deposit as the compensating control and an expiry date of 31 January 2027.
Three of four milestones were subsequently met. The reconciliation milestone remains outstanding as of
September 2026, and weekly settlement has accordingly not been granted. The exception is operating as intended: the commercial benefit was delivered where it was safe to do so, and the financial control held.

4.2 Computation
R-4. Settlement is computed from order, return and refund events. Those events are the source of truth.
Where the ledger and the event history disagree, the event history governs.
R-5. Every ledger entry must be uniquely identifiable by a business key. Reversal entries are order-scoped and their uniqueness key must include the order identifier.
R-6. Batch reprocessing requires an explicit replay authorisation with a documented reason. Idempotency of the computation is not sufficient justification to rerun a batch without authorisation.
R-7. Ledger invariant checks must pass before payout is authorised. At minimum: each reversal maps to exactly one originating order line; entry types sum to the batch net; no entry appears more than once under its composite key.
R-8. A schema or migration change affecting a key, constraint or uniqueness guarantee on financial data requires financial review in addition to engineering review.
4.3 Variance Detection
R-9. Each cycle must be compared against a payout predicted independently from source events before funds are released.
R-10. A variance exceeding 0.75 percent or INR 50,000, whichever is lower in absolute terms, raises an operations alert and blocks payout pending review.
R-11. A variance detected after payout is handled as a financial recovery under the Payment and Settlement
Recovery Runbook.
Rules R-9 and R-10 were introduced in version 3.1 after a settlement shortfall in March 2026 was detected by a seller's own reconciliation rather than by any platform control. The policy previously assumed the ledger was correct and provided no mechanism to test that assumption.

5. Tax Documents
R-12. Tax invoices and credit notes generated by the platform are the platform's responsibility. The platform is accountable for the correctness of the rate, the classification and the document itself.
R-13. A listing whose tax category resolves to a category default rather than to an explicit mapping must not be published. It is held for classification.
R-14. Where an incorrect rate has been applied, a credit note is issued against each incorrect invoice and the invoice is re-issued at the correct rate. A net adjustment line is not an acceptable correction for a tax error, because the counterparty requires a corrective document per invoice for its own filing.
R-15. Where a rate revision is applied, the completeness of the remap must be verified for both existing and subsequently created listings.
R-16. The cost of correcting a platform-generated tax error is borne by the platform. It is not recovered from the seller or from the buyer.

R-17. Refund processing must be idempotent. A refund event that has already been applied must not be applied again, regardless of delivery semantics upstream.
R-18. Any consumer of an at-least-once event stream that performs a non-idempotent financial operation must maintain an idempotency record. This is a design review gate, not a recommendation.
R-19. Duplicate refunds are reversed at the payment processor where the transaction is unsettled. Where settled, the amount is pursued only where material and proportionate; otherwise it is written off with a named approver.
R-20. Refund volume per account must be monitored against expected volume, with alerting on material deviation.
7. Recovery of Overpayments
R-21. Where a seller has been overpaid through platform error, recovery is staged across settlement cycles by default. A single debit is used only at the seller's request.
R-22. No interest or fee is applied where the seller did not cause the error.
R-23. Recovery terms are a Business decision. Operations executes; Operations does not decide who bears a cost.
R-24. Where recovery cost exceeds the amount recoverable, the amount is written off with a documented rationale and a named approver.

1. Purpose
This policy defines who may access which enterprise information, on what basis, and how that access is granted, reviewed and revoked.
The platform holds seller-specific commercial, technical and financial information. Access to it is governed by two independent dimensions: seller scope, which determines which accounts an identity may see, and clearance, which determines the sensitivity level an identity may read. Both must be satisfied for access to be granted.
2. Scope

4. Access Principles
Page 1 of 5

P-1. Least privilege. Access is granted for a defined work purpose and reviewed quarterly. It is not granted for convenience or seniority.
P-2. Two-dimensional. Scope and clearance are independent. No clearance level grants cross-portfolio access, and no scope grants access above the holder's clearance.
P-3. Work allocation, not hierarchy. Scope derives from the accounts an identity actually works on.
P-4. Deny by default. Absence of an explicit grant is a denial.
P-5. No implicit elevation. An identity acting on a shared component does not thereby gain scope.
Engineering work on a platform-wide defect across all sellers grants visibility into the defect record, not into each affected seller's account documents.
P-5 is a deliberate restriction and a common source of confusion. An engineer remediating a platform defect affecting twelve accounts can see the defect record and the technical detail, but not the commercial account documents for accounts outside their scope. Where account-specific detail is required for remediation, it is provided through a scoped extract rather than by widening scope.

1. Purpose
This policy governs the suspension of seller accounts, the automated risk rules that trigger suspension, the review process, and the conditions for reinstatement.
Its governing principle: suspension exists to protect customers from harm arising from seller conduct. It is not a mechanism for recovering platform costs, and it must not penalise a seller for the consequences of a platform defect.

1. Purpose
This policy defines how security incidents are detected, classified, contained, investigated and closed. It covers credential exposure, unauthorised access, suspected data exposure and security-relevant misconfiguration.
Its guiding principle is that containment takes precedence over investigation, and that an exposed credential is treated as compromised regardless of evidence about whether it was used.
2. Scope
Applies to any actual or suspected security event affecting platform systems, seller data, customer data or credentials.
Applies to events detected internally, reported by a seller, or reported by a third party such as a payment processor or logistics provider.
Does not cover availability incidents with no security dimension, which follow the Incident Escalation
Procedure.
3. Definitions
Term
Definition
Security incident
Any event affecting confidentiality, integrity or access control
Credential exposure
A credential that has become accessible outside its intended custodians
Containment
Action that stops the exposure from being exploitable
Evidence of unauthorised access or use
Suspected compromise

Blast radius
The set of systems, records and accounts potentially affected
4. Classification
R-1. Every security incident is classified at least RESTRICTED at creation, regardless of assessed severity.
Reclassification downward requires Platform Administrator approval and a recorded rationale.
R-2. Every security incident is SEV-1 by default, regardless of confirmed impact.
R-3. Severity may be reduced after containment where the blast radius is established and no compromise is found. Reduction is recorded with reasoning.
Page 1 of 4

R-4. A confirmed compromise involving customer data, payment data or credentials with write access to seller commercial data is escalated to the Platform Administrator and Business immediately.
5. Response Procedure
Step 1 - Report
R-5. Any identity who suspects a security incident must report it to IT immediately. Reporting must not wait for confirmation.
R-6. A person who reports promptly is treated as having acted correctly, regardless of how the exposure occurred. The response addresses the cause, not the reporter.
Step 2 - Contain
R-7. The Platform Administrator may authorise immediate containment, including credential rotation, without seller consent and without waiting for seller readiness.
R-8. Containment must not be delayed to establish whether the exposure was exploited. Exploitation is established, if at all, during investigation.
R-9. Where containment interrupts a seller's service, the interruption is accepted where the alternative risk is larger. Fees and service credits do not apply to a containment action initiated under this policy.
In April 2026, rotating a compromised credential broke a seller's feeds for 80 minutes. The alternative was leaving an unknown party holding a valid credential with write access to 142,000 listings. Rotation was authorised within 35 minutes of the exposure being located.
Step 3 - Establish Blast Radius
R-10. Determine: which credential or access path, which systems, which accounts, and which time window.
R-11. Review authentication and access logs for the period before exposure was detected, not only after.
R-12. A log review finding no evidence of use is recorded as absence of evidence, never as evidence that access did not occur.
Step 4 - Investigate
R-13. Investigate how the exposure occurred, not only what was exposed. The mechanism determines the preventive action.
R-14. Investigate whether the exposure was systematic. A credential in a shared script usually indicates a practice rather than a single lapse.
R-15. Review whether a similar exposure exists elsewhere. Where one credential is found, sweep for others before closing.
Step 5 - Remediate
R-16. Rotate every exposed credential. Treat all as compromised.
R-17. Where a credential was shared across environments, issue separate credentials.
R-18. Apply the preventive controls identified, with owners and dates.
R-19. Preserve evidence until the incident is closed and any review is complete.
Step 6 - Notify
R-20. The affected seller is told what happened to the extent it affects them, including any action required,
without disclosing the classification framework or the controls bypassed.
Page 2 of 4

R-21. Customer notification is assessed by the Platform Administrator and Business together, where customer data is potentially involved. Notification is made where required by law or where notification reduces customer harm.
R-22. Where a third party is involved, for example a provider whose API was compromised, coordination is led by IT.
Step 7 - Close
R-23. An incident may be closed where containment is complete, the blast radius is established, preventive actions have owners and dates, and the affected seller has been notified of the outcome.
R-24. A security incident is not closed at containment. Log review and preventive action completion are required.

1. Purpose
This policy defines how confidential and restricted information is created, stored, shared, transmitted and destroyed. It applies to information about sellers, customers, employees and the platform itself.
Its purpose is to make handling requirements explicit, so that a person handling a record does not have to infer the correct behaviour from its sensitivity.
2. Scope
Applies to all employees, contractors and service accounts handling any platform information.
Applies to all formats: documents, database records, tickets, transcripts, messages, code, configuration and diagnostic output.
3. Definitions
Term
Definition
Confidential information
Any record classified CONFIDENTIAL or RESTRICTED
Credential
Any secret used for authentication: password, key, token, secret
Diagnostic artefact
A script, log extract, query or output produced while investigating an issue
External sharing
Any transmission outside the company, including to a seller
At rest
Stored on any medium
In transit

4. General Rules
R-1. Confidential information is accessed only where required for a work purpose, and only within the access model in the Data Access Policy.
R-2. Confidential information is not copied to personal devices, personal accounts or unmanaged storage.
R-3. Sharing externally requires authorisation from the record owner and must be limited to the minimum content necessary for the stated purpose.
R-4. Where information is shared with a seller, it is limited to the seller's own account. A seller must never receive another seller's information, including in aggregate form where the aggregate would disclose it.
5. Credential Handling
Page 1 of 4

R-5. Credentials are never embedded in source code, scripts, configuration files committed to version control, tickets, documentation or messages.
R-6. Credentials are resolved at runtime from the credential store. A person or process requiring a credential obtains it through the store, not from a stored value in another artefact.
R-7. The distinction between staging and production credentials is not a distinction an attacker respects. No diagnostic artefact containing any credential may be shared outside the company, regardless of the environment the credential belongs to.
R-8. Separate credentials must be issued for staging and production. A shared credential is prohibited.
R-9. All machine credentials are enrolled in automated rotation with a maximum age of 90 days.
R-10. Suspected credential exposure is treated as SEV-1 and escalated to IT immediately, without waiting to establish whether the credential is still valid.
Rule R-7 exists because of a specific failure. In April 2026 a support engineer shared a diagnostic script externally believing the credential it contained was a staging credential. The account used the same credential for staging and production, so it was in fact production-scoped and permitted write access to a seller's catalogue and price feed. The credential had not been rotated in 46 months.
6. Diagnostic Artefacts
R-11. Diagnostic tooling for seller integrations is provided centrally and resolves credentials from the store at runtime. Support engineers must not handle raw credential values.
R-12. Where an ad hoc script is unavoidable, it must not contain any connection detail, and it must be deleted after use rather than retained.
R-13. Diagnostic output containing seller data is classified at least CONFIDENTIAL and is stored only in approved locations. Extracts must not be left in shared directories or email.
R-14. Log extracts shared for troubleshooting must be reviewed to remove credentials, tokens and personal data before transmission, including transmission to a seller.
7. Storage and Transmission
R-15. Confidential information is stored in approved systems: the document store, the ticket system, the incident system or the approved data platform. It must not be stored in ad hoc locations.
R-16. Transmission of confidential information outside approved systems requires encryption and authorised recipients.
R-17. RESTRICTED information must not be reproduced in a lower-classified record. A reference may be made; the content must not.
A RESTRICTED incident record may be referenced from a CONFIDENTIAL ticket so that a reader knows it exists and who owns it. The RESTRICTED record's contents - credential detail, thresholds, risk determinations - must not be copied into the CONFIDENTIAL record, because that would defeat the classification.
R-18. Screenshots of confidential records are treated as confidential records and are subject to the same storage rules.
8. Retention and Destruction

R-19. Confidential information is retained only for the period defined in the Data Retention Policy, after which it is destroyed or de-identified.
R-20. Destruction is performed through an approved mechanism. Deleting a record from an application is not destruction where a backup retains it; the retention schedule governs.
R-21. Diagnostic artefacts are temporary by nature and must be deleted immediately after the investigation concludes.
