Decision: re-issue credit notes for all 1,240 affected invoices, absorb the reconciliation difference of INR
2,17,600 at platform cost, and add a mandatory tax mapping validation to the listing workflow.
2. Context
On 24 February 2026 Aurelia's finance team reported that invoices for decorative lighting SKUs listed since 1
February 2026 had been issued at an 18 percent tax rate rather than 12 percent. Support raised the ticket the same day and confirmed the pattern across 1,240 invoices.
The cause was a mapping gap rather than a calculation defect. Following an HSN revision, the 12 percent slab applied to a subset of decorative lighting products. Existing SKUs were remapped as part of the revision, but SKUs created after the revision were assigned the category default, which remained 18 percent.
Aurelia is unusually exposed to this class of error because it files GST returns using platform-generated invoices directly. An incorrect rate is not merely a reporting inconvenience; it produces an incorrect filing.
3. Options Considered
Option A - Re-issue credit notes and correct mapping at platform cost
Issue credit notes against the 1,240 incorrect invoices, re-issue at the correct rate, and absorb the INR
2,17,600 difference rather than recovering it from the seller or the buyer.
 Restores the seller's filing position for the February period.
 Highest immediate cost to the platform.
 Cleanest audit trail: one corrective transaction per invoice.
Page 1 of 3

Option B - Adjust prospectively and net the difference in settlement
Correct the mapping going forward and recover or credit the difference as a single settlement adjustment line, without re-issuing invoices.
 Cheaper to execute and faster.
 Leaves 1,240 incorrect tax documents in the seller's records.
 Rejected: it does not resolve the seller's filing exposure, which is the substance of the problem.
Option C - Ask the seller to raise buyer-level corrections
Place the correction burden on Aurelia.
 Lowest platform cost.
 Rejected: the defect was platform-side, and the Payment and Settlement
Policy (POL-FIN-002) places responsibility for the accuracy of platform-generated tax documents on the platform.
4. Decision and Rationale
Option A was approved. The determining factor was responsibility rather than cost: the tax document is generated by the platform, so its accuracy is a platform obligation under the Payment and Settlement Policy
(POL-FIN-002). Recovering the difference from a seller who did not cause the error would have been inconsistent with that obligation and would have damaged a Gold-tier relationship over a sum that is immaterial at platform level.
A secondary consideration was timing. February is a filing month. Delaying a decision to negotiate cost-sharing would have pushed the correction past Aurelia's filing deadline and converted a recoverable error into a compliance problem for the seller.

6. Technical Design Summary
6.1 Inventory
Aurelia's ERP emits a stock movement event on every pick, receipt and adjustment. A lightweight adapter translates these into Seller API v2 stock update calls. The adapter batches movements within a 30-second window to avoid excessive call volume on high-velocity SKUs, which keeps publication well inside the
60-second target.
Page 2 of 4

A reconciliation job runs nightly and compares Aurelia's authoritative stock position against published availability. Any SKU with a variance is logged and re-pushed. This job is the control that makes the real-time path trustworthy.
6.2 Orders
Orders are delivered by webhook with an HMAC signature. The receiver acknowledges within two seconds and processes asynchronously. Because webhook delivery is at-least-once, the receiver deduplicates on order identifier before creating an ERP order.
The deduplication requirement was specified explicitly here because at-least-once delivery is a platform-wide characteristic. The same class of requirement is revisited in later platform work on refund processing.
A polling fallback runs every 15 minutes and fetches any order not seen by the webhook path in the previous
30 minutes.
6.3 Settlement
Aurelia retrieves a settlement report per cycle through the report endpoint. The report includes gross value,
commission, reversals, adjustments and net payable, at order-line granularity. Aurelia's finance system matches this against its own order export and flags any line with a variance above one percent.

3.1 WS-1 Ledger Invariant Checks
A set of invariants now runs against every settlement batch before payout is authorised. The checks confirm that each reversal entry maps to exactly one originating order line, that the sum of entry types reconciles to the batch net, and that no entry appears more than once under its composite key.
The invariant that would have caught SC-001 is the third one. It was back-tested against twelve months of historical batches and found two further low-value anomalies from 2025, both since corrected.
3.2 WS-2 Automated Variance Detection
Each cycle is compared against a predicted payout derived from order and return events. Any seller whose variance exceeds 0.75 percent, or INR 50,000 in absolute terms, raises an operations alert before payout rather than after.
Since go-live on 10 July 2026 the control has raised four alerts across all sellers. Three were legitimate commercial adjustments. One, on 14 August 2026, was a genuine mapping error on a different account and was corrected before payout.
3.3 WS-3 Reprocessing Safety Controls
The trigger condition in SC-001 was a reprocessing run after a transient job failure. Reprocessing is now idempotent by construction: a batch carries a processing token, and a second run with the same token is rejected unless an operator explicitly authorises a replay with a documented reason.

3.1 WS-A Load Shedding and Backpressure
Delivered on 26 August 2026, two days early.
 Circuit breaker on the inventory lookup path, opening at a 25 percent error rate over a 10-second window, with a 30-second half-open probe.

 Overload responses changed from HTTP 503 to HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header, making the correct client behaviour explicit.
 Request-level timeout of 2.5 seconds on the order placement path.
Validation: a synthetic retry storm at four times observed July peak was run on 24 August 2026. The service shed load at 429 and recovered within 40 seconds of the storm ending, with no pool exhaustion.

2. The Request
On 15 January 2026 Ananya Rao, co-founder of GreenCart Organics, requested:
1. Immediate upgrade from Silver to Gold tier.
2. Weekly settlement instead of fortnightly, effective immediately.
3. Gold-tier commission banding applied from February 2026.
The stated reason was cash flow. GreenCart buys perishable stock on short payment terms from farm suppliers and sells on a subscription model. A fortnightly settlement cycle with a T+2 payout means up to 16
days between delivering goods and receiving funds, which the seller described as the binding constraint on its growth.
3. Policy Position
The Seller Onboarding Policy ties settlement frequency to a readiness assessment rather than to tier alone.
Weekly settlement requires:
 Six consecutive cycles with no settlement dispute.
 Automated order and refund reconciliation at the seller's end.
Page 1 of 3

 A verified failover configuration for fulfilment-critical integrations.
 Dispute rate below the category threshold.
At the time of the request GreenCart had completed four settlement cycles, had no automated reconciliation,
and had an unverified failover configuration carried over as open item OI-1 from onboarding. It met the dispute rate condition comfortably.
So the request could not be approved as submitted. The question was whether to refuse, defer, or approve with conditions.
4. Options Considered
Option A - Refuse until all conditions are met
Predictable and consistent with policy. Estimated timeline to natural compliance was five to six months,
which the seller indicated would force a reduction in its subscription base.
Option B - Approve in full as a commercial exception
Fast and commercially attractive. Rejected on risk grounds: weekly settlement on an account with no automated reconciliation and an unverified fulfilment failover concentrates platform exposure precisely where this seller is weakest.
Option C - Conditional upgrade with phased milestones
Grant the tier upgrade immediately, which carries commission and visibility benefits, but tie the settlement frequency change to specific, verifiable milestones. Secure the interim exposure with a deposit.
5. Decision and Rationale
Option C was approved on 20 January 2026.
The reasoning was that the tier upgrade and the settlement change carry different risks. Tier affects commission banding and merchandising treatment; if the seller underperforms, the platform can reverse it at the next review with no financial exposure. Settlement frequency affects how much unreconciled value the platform pays out before a dispute could surface, and that exposure is not reversible in the same way.
Separating the two allowed the commercial benefit to be delivered immediately while keeping the financial control intact.
The INR 3,00,000 deposit was sized against the largest single-cycle dispute observed on comparable accounts, not against GreenCart's cycle value. It is refundable once all milestones are validated.

1. Purpose
This document covers the onboarding of GreenCart Organics Pvt. Ltd. (S003), a subscription-first organic grocery business, and records the closure position handed to the account team. GreenCart was the first perishable-category seller onboarded on the platform, so several standard onboarding assumptions had to be varied.
2. What Made This Onboarding Different
Three characteristics separated GreenCart from previous onboardings.
Perishable goods. A missed delivery slot is a write-off, not a reschedule. Standard dispatch SLA definitions,
which assume a failed delivery can be retried the next day, do not hold. Fulfilment requirements were therefore expressed against delivery slots rather than against dispatch windows.
Subscription ordering. GreenCart's customers buy a recurring weekly basket. Orders arrive in predictable batches tied to slot cut-offs rather than being distributed through the day. Capacity planning is concentrated rather than smooth, and a failure at a slot cut-off affects an entire cohort at once.
Connector-based integration. GreenCart runs its storefront on Shopify and did not have the engineering capacity to build a direct integration. A connector bridge was used instead, which shortened the project considerably but introduced a translation layer between Shopify objects and Seller API calls.

1. Scope of These Notes
These notes describe how GreenCart Organics (S003) is technically integrated with the platform, and record the behaviour of the integration during the two production incidents on this account in 2026. They are written for engineers who need to reason about where a fault lies when GreenCart reports a problem.
The central point is that GreenCart's integration has three layers, and most confusion on this account comes from attributing a fault to the wrong one.

2. Order Intake Path
An order placed on the marketplace is delivered to the connector by webhook. The connector translates it into a Shopify order object, applies the delivery slot as a line-item property, and acknowledges. GreenCart's dark store systems read from Shopify.
Important characteristics:
 Delivery is at-least-once. The connector deduplicates on the platform order identifier before creating a Shopify order.
 Slot metadata travels as a line-item property, not as an order-level field.
This was a Shopify modelling constraint and is the reason the pilot found an amendment defect in August
2025.
 Acknowledgement is fast and processing is asynchronous, so a slow Shopify
API does not cause webhook retries at the platform end.
3. Inventory Path
Stock is maintained per dark store. The connector publishes availability at slot granularity: a SKU can be available for tomorrow's morning slot and unavailable for tonight's, because stock is allocated against slot capacity rather than against a single pool.
Page 1 of 3

This is unlike any other account on the platform. S001 and S002 publish a single availability figure per SKU
per location. Engineers investigating a GreenCart availability question should not assume the S002 model applies.
4. Label Generation Path
Every dispatch requires a shipping label from the Shipment Label Service. The service is configured with a primary courier provider (SwiftLane) and a backup (RapidPost).
4.1 Behaviour Observed in SC-005, 18 June 2026
SwiftLane's API degraded during the morning slot cut-off. The expected behaviour was automatic failover to
RapidPost. Failover did not occur.
The reason was that the stored RapidPost credentials had expired. The failover path attempted to authenticate at the moment failover was needed, the authentication failed, and the service fell back to retrying the primary provider rather than surfacing a credential error. 2,100 orders were left in label-pending state and 640 perishable orders breached their delivery slot.
Three engineering observations from that incident are worth recording.
1. The failover path was never exercised in production before it was needed,
so an expired credential was indistinguishable from a working configuration.
2. Failing back to the degraded primary provider was worse than failing loudly.
The system preserved the appearance of function while producing no labels.
3. Credential expiry was observable in the credential store but was not monitored.
Remediation: credentials rotated, an automated expiry monitor added covering both providers, and a failover pre-flight check that validates backup credentials on a schedule rather than at the moment of need.
5. Refund Path
Refunds originate either from a platform-side action or from GreenCart's refund-on-report process for quality complaints. Both produce a refund event on the event bus, consumed by the refund webhook consumer.
5.1 Behaviour Observed in SC-007, 3 September 2026
The refund webhook consumer restarted during a deployment. The broker redelivered events that had been processed but not acknowledged. Because the consumer applied refunds without checking an idempotency key, 640 refunds were applied twice, an excess of INR 1,18,000.
GreenCart was disproportionately exposed to this defect for a structural reason: the refund-on-report category exception means this account generates a far higher ratio of refund events to orders than any other seller. The defect was platform-wide, but it surfaced here first and hardest.
Remediation: an idempotency store keyed on refund event identifier, with a retention window of 30 days;
duplicate refunds reversed; consumer replay guarded; and a duplication alert configured on refund volume per account.
The requirement to tolerate at-least-once delivery was written into the S002 integration specification as
ORD-3 and into the S001 integration design in 2023. The refund consumer predates both and was never revisited. This is a documentation and inventory problem as much as a coding defect.

Either condition alone would have produced a review flag. Both together triggered automatic suspension without human review, which is the designed behaviour of the rule.
3. Review Findings
3.1 The Return Rate Was Platform-Caused
The elevated return rate is attributable to the size chart defect recorded in SC-006. A schema update to the dropship feed importer on 14 July 2026 applied the UK-to-EU size conversion twice, publishing size charts two sizes smaller than the physical product. Customers received footwear that did not fit and returned it. The
Page 1 of 3

dominant return reason code across the period was size-too-small.
StrideOne did not author the defective data, could not have detected it from its own systems, and reported the pattern to Support on 5 August 2026, which is how the defect was found.
3.2 The Chargeback Ratio Was Downstream of the Same Cause
The chargeback ratio rose because a proportion of customers who received the wrong size initiated a payment dispute rather than a return, particularly where the return window had lapsed while they sought an exchange. The ratio is therefore a second-order effect of the same defect.
3.3 The Metric Lagged the Fix
Corrected size charts were published on 19 August 2026. By the week ending 6 September the weekly return rate had fallen to 13 percent. The risk rule evaluated a trailing 30-day average, which still included the peak weeks.
The rule suspended an account for a condition that had been resolved three weeks earlier.
3.4 No Evidence of Seller Conduct Issues
Review of the account found no misrepresentation, no counterfeit reports, no partner compliance findings and no pattern of customer complaints unrelated to sizing. Order defect rate excluding size-related returns was 4.1 percent, within the Gold tier threshold.
4. Decision and Rationale
The suspension was lifted at 16:40 IST on 10 September 2026.
The rationale is that the Account Suspension Policy exists to protect customers from seller conduct that creates harm. It is not intended to penalise a seller for the consequences of a platform defect. Applying it here would have transferred the cost of a platform engineering error onto a seller who reported that error.
Three further determinations were made.
1. The suspension is recorded in the account risk history as platform-caused and is excluded from future risk assessment for this account.
2. Commercial consequences arising from the suspension are waived: the returns reserve adjustment is reversed and reverse logistics cost for the affected period is absorbed by the platform.
3. The triggering rule is recalibrated before it can suspend this account again; until recalibration is complete, any S004 suspension requires manual review.

Back-tested against the July 2026 feed, the rule would have rejected the import on the day the defect was deployed.

1. Purpose
This document records the onboarding of StrideOne Footwear Pvt. Ltd. (S004) and the delivery of its dropship integration. StrideOne holds no inventory of its own; orders are routed to third-party logistics partners who hold brand stock. The integration therefore had to solve a routing problem and a catalogue problem that earlier onboardings did not present.
2. The Dropship Model
In a conventional marketplace integration the seller owns stock, knows where it is, and dispatches it.
StrideOne owns none of these things.
 Stock is held by four third-party logistics partners, each with its own systems and its own view of availability.
 Product data originates with the partners, not with StrideOne.
 Dispatch is performed by the partner, so StrideOne never physically inspects a product before it reaches a customer.
 Returns are received by the partner, so return reason data flows back through the partner rather than from StrideOne.
The practical consequence is that StrideOne's listing quality is a function of partner-supplied data. The platform's published product specification, including the size chart, is derived from a feed the seller does not author.

4. Integration Design
4.1 Order Routing
An order line is routed to a partner based on declared availability, delivery geography and partner SLA.
Routing is evaluated at order placement, not at dispatch, so a partner stock-out after routing produces a cancellation rather than a re-route. This was accepted at design time as a simplification; it remains the largest known weakness in the design.
4.2 Product Feed
Partners deliver product data on a schedule. The feed importer normalises brand, colour, material and size attributes into the platform catalogue schema.
Size is the most complex normalisation. Partners supply sizes in UK, EU or US conventions depending on brand, and the importer converts to a single published size chart. The conversion table is maintained by the platform.
This conversion is the component that failed in August 2026, when a schema update caused the UK-to-EU
conversion to be applied twice. The design note below was written at onboarding and proved prescient.
Design note from August 2025, recorded verbatim in the original plan:
"Size conversion is the only transformation in this feed that cannot be validated by inspecting a single record.
A wrong colour is obvious; a wrong size is only detectable by comparing the published chart against the physical product or against return data. Validation must therefore be structural rather than per-record."
The structural validation implied by that note was not implemented at onboarding. It was deferred as open item OI-2 and delivered only in August 2026 after the defect occurred.
4.3 Returns
Return reason codes flow from the partner to the platform. The codes relevant to this account are size-too-small, size-too-large, not-as-described and quality. Return rate is monitored because it drives both reverse logistics cost and, through the risk rules engine, account standing.

Cause
An unbounded client retry policy generated a retry storm. Combined with a missing circuit breaker on the inventory lookup path, the order service connection pool was exhausted: healthy requests could not obtain a connection because the pool was full of retries waiting on a slow dependency.
The platform contributed the missing circuit breaker and an inadequate pool configuration. The client contributed the unbounded retries. Neither side alone would have produced a 40-minute degradation.
Post-Incident Discussion
The 17 July call was direct. Sameer's initial position was that the platform had failed to handle his traffic.
Engineering's position was that the traffic had been amplified by his retry policy and that no capacity figure would have been sufficient against an unbounded retry loop.
Page 2 of 3

Both were right, and the call ended with a shared workstream rather than an argument about blame:
 Platform: circuit breaker, pool resizing, request timeouts, and a change from HTTP 503 to HTTP 429 with Retry-After so correct client behaviour is explicit.
 BluePeak: bounded retries with exponential backoff and jitter, honour
Retry-After, add a client-side circuit breaker.
 Both: a 10-working-day capacity notice before any promotional event, which is now a contractual expectation on this account.
Resolution
Emergency mitigation restored service within 37 minutes of the seller's call. 1,120 failed orders were replayed on 18 July where the cart was still valid. Permanent remediation is tracked in the S002 throughput and resilience programme and was verified by a synthetic retry storm at four times observed peak on 24

This was the substance of the ticket, more than the technical cause.
Operations decided that the excess INR 1,18,000 would be recovered across four settlement cycles rather than in a single deduction, and that no interest or fee would apply. The reasoning was that the seller did not cause the error and a single large debit on a cash-constrained account would have caused real operational harm for no benefit to the platform.
Customers who received a duplicate refund were not asked to return it. The duplicated amounts were reversed at the payment-processor level where the transaction had not yet settled, which covered 412 of the
640 cases. For the remaining 228, the amount was written off rather than pursued, on cost and proportionality grounds.

The suspension was lifted at 16:40 on 10 September after a formal review by Operations. The review found no seller conduct issue, attributed the return rate to the platform-side defect, and recorded the suspension as platform-caused so that it does not count against future risk assessment.

Process Failures Worth Recording
Three things went wrong here beyond the risk rule itself.
1. No human in the loop before a full revenue stop. The account went from trading to fully suspended at 02:14 with no prior warning and no named contact.
2. The notification was useless. It told the seller they were suspended pending review. It did not say which metric, which threshold, which window, or who to contact.
3. The rule had no knowledge of the defect. The platform had an open record showing that this seller's return rate was inflated by a platform defect. The rule could not see it.
All three are addressed in the corrective actions attached to DR-2026-047. A manual review gate is active for this account until the rule recalibration completes.

1. Company Overview
Nexora Commerce Pvt. Ltd. operates Nexora Marketplace, a multi-category online marketplace headquartered in Bengaluru, Karnataka, India. The company was founded in 2019 and connects third-party sellers with retail customers across India. Sellers list catalogues on the platform, receive orders through platform integrations, fulfil those orders either from their own warehouses or through logistics partners, and are paid through a scheduled settlement cycle.
The platform is organised around a small number of core services. The Catalog Service holds listings and attributes. The Order Service accepts and routes orders. The Inventory Sync Service keeps seller stock levels aligned with published listings. The Settlement and Payout Service computes seller earnings,
deductions and reversals. The Invoicing Service issues tax documents. Fulfilment integrations connect the platform to courier partners. An event bus carries order, refund and settlement events between services.
Because sellers differ substantially in size, business model and integration maturity, knowledge about a seller accumulates in different places: account documents owned by Business, tickets owned by Support,
incident reports owned by Engineering, runbooks and recovery records owned by Operations, and access and security records owned by IT. This document defines the organisational model that governs who may read which part of that knowledge.

Account Managers hold a named portfolio of sellers, negotiate commercial terms, maintain account overviews and decision records, and represent the seller internally during escalations. Engineering owns platform services and their reliability. Operations owns runbooks and procedures, and it is accountable for confirming that a recovery actually restored correct data,
not merely that a service returned to health.

IT owns identity, access administration, security monitoring and platform administration. The Platform
Administrator maintains user records, seller scope assignments and clearance levels, and leads security incident handling together with Engineering.

5.1 How Classification Is Decided
General operational instructions that describe how the company works are INTERNAL, because any employee may need them and they contain no seller-identifying commercial data. The Seller Onboarding
Runbook and the Deployment Rollback Procedure are examples.
Anything naming a specific seller together with commercial, financial or defect detail is at least
CONFIDENTIAL. Settlement amounts, return rates, ticket histories and incident impact figures fall in this category.
Material that would materially assist an attacker, or that records a security event, credential handling detail or an account risk determination, is RESTRICTED. The credential exposure incident of April 2026 and the account suspension review of September 2026 are handled at this level, as is the access-control detail inside the Data Access Policy.

The suspension was lifted on 10 September 2026, a corrective action plan was agreed, and the risk rule was recalibrated to take known platform defects into account. Estimated lost sales during the suspension were INR 6,40,000 per day.
SC-006 and SC-012 are the clearest example in this dataset of one event causing another across departmental boundaries: an Engineering defect produced an Operations risk determination with commercial consequences.
